A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same sparse-autoencoder amortisation-gap study. Their text, equations, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across the changed layout and appendix numbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic sparse-recovery experiments, GPT-2 feature-interpretability results, and appendix ablations and dictionary-learning comparisons.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds larger-scale and Zipfian synthetic experiments, an expanded GPT-2 comparison, and scored feature examples.

M1.justification: The decoupled encoding/decoding framework and the four core procedures in Section 3.3 remain unchanged. LCA is introduced as an evaluated comparator; the wider MLP is an experimental configuration change. Newly documented implementation details do not establish a revised core algorithm.

E1.justification: Appendix D adds synthetic scenarios with Zipf-distributed feature activation probabilities and magnitudes, extending coverage beyond the original distribution. OpenWebText, GPT-2 Small Layer 9, and the sparse-recovery tasks remain. Appendix C increases dimensionality and sample count within existing task coverage.

E2.justification: Section 5 and Figure 7 add the locally competitive algorithm (LCA) to the previously SAE-versus-MLP GPT-2 comparison. The existing synthetic comparators, including SAE+ITO, sparse coding, and the appendix LARS comparison, are retained.

E3.justification: The GPT-2 MLP width changes from 4224 to 8448, the interpretability evaluator from GPT-4 to GPT-4o, and the stated feature sample from 200 to 500 per method. Appendix C introduces a larger experiment with 500,000 samples, 20,000 steps, and minibatches of 1024. Section 3.2 also removes Gaussian noise from the stated observation model; this documents a setting revision without establishing which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendices C and D test persistence of the amortisation gap at larger scale and robustness to unequal feature frequencies and magnitudes across recovery scenarios. Table 1 adds concrete interpreted-feature examples. Earlier decoder-weight, MLP-width, bias, and top-k analyses remain under new numbering.

E5.justification: Section 5 adds a Kruskal-Wallis test and Dunn’s pairwise tests with Bonferroni correction to the previously descriptive interpretability comparison. The five-independent-run statement in Section 4.3 is unchanged. The new tests’ sample basis is unclear because the text and caption specify 500 features per method while Figure 7 labels N=2500.

E6.justification: Section 5 replaces reconstruction, sparsity, dead-feature, and interpretability results under revised settings. Figure 7’s annotated SAE/MLP F1 summaries are 0.64/0.69 in v1 and 0.63/0.83 in v2, which also reports LCA at 0.61. Figures 8-11 add larger-scale and Zipfian results, and Table 1 adds six scored interpretations. These are new or replaced results, not controlled performance gains over v1.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.1 adds the assumption that the source distribution’s support forms a union of K-dimensional subspaces, absent from v1’s theorem. The rank/ReLU proof remains substantively unchanged. The restated theorem in v2 Appendix A still omits the added assumption, leaving the formal statements inconsistent.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction strengthen the practical claim from comparable interpretability to greater interpretability from more expressive encoders. The discussion now claims MLP features outperform both SAE and LCA features. Conversely, synthetic superiority is qualified to sparse coding and only sometimes MLPs, while the central amortisation-gap contribution remains.

C2.justification: New Appendix B interprets the theorem as an impossibility of recovering every feasible code, distinguishing local, probabilistic, and iterative recovery guarantees. Appendices C-D add explanations involving dimensional interference and hierarchical features. The discussion adds limitations concerning LCA optimisation and sampling only highly activating examples, alongside a stronger explanation linking encoder complexity to feature quality.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents Adam, dead-column resampling every 15,000 steps, LCA’s 100 inference steps per batch, and its 10^-5 activation threshold. Appendices C-D specify minibatch settings and Zipf parameter alpha=1. Existing FLOP calculations and interpretability prompts remain; the added disclosures do not establish that every previously unspecified implementation choice changed.

R1.justification: New Appendix B substantially positions the impossibility result against Rangamani et al. (2018), Nguyen et al. (2019), and iterative LISTA approaches. New RIP and heavy-tailed-representation citations support the expanded discussion. The historical distributed-representation survey and its associated references disappear with v1’s Conceptual Modelling Framework appendix.

P1.justification: The abstract and Sections 2.4, 5, and 6 are rewritten or condensed, the conceptual-framework appendix is removed, and new appendices are inserted. Alim Gumran is added as an author. The six-section main structure and much of the methods, proof, and retained appendix prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: The document is comprehensively reformatted from one column to two, substantially changing figure placement, sizing, and equation layout. The conceptual-framework illustration is removed; four experimental figures and Table 1 are added; Figure 7 expands to three groups. Existing appendix plots are largely retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: The added scale and distribution tests, broader GPT-2 comparison, and clearer theoretical positioning address useful gaps in v1. However, Figure 7’s unresolved 500-versus-2500 sample discrepancy weakens the new statistical evidence, and Appendix D claims higher known-code MCC under Zipf sampling although Figures 2 and 9 show the opposite. These problems affect important new evidence, making the net quality benefit uncertain.
